newsitem.title: TURKEY: Riding high, Turk Islamists push social agenda.
newsitem.headline: Riding high, Turk Islamists push social agenda.

text.p: Turkey's Islamists, emboldened after seven months in power, have returned to their grassroots with crowd-pleasing calls for more Islamic veiling of women and opening of a "superhighway" to Mecca.

Analysts say favourable economic news and persistent political problems for his pro-Western coalition partner, have made Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan confident enough to take on the secularist elite, including the armed forces.
At the same time, the possibility of early polls has forced Erbakan's Welfare Party to woo the religious and protest votes that gave him a narrow plurality in general polls in December of 1995.

The result is a flurry of proposals during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan to return Welfare to its religious roots: lifting the ban on Islamic headscarves for women civil servants and paving the road for overland pilgrimages to the Moslem holy city of Mecca.
Other measures include construction of mosques in historic secularist strongholds, including the Christian quarter of the former Ottoman capital.
"We will finish the conquest of Istanbul," said an exultant Erbakan, announcing plans for a massive mosque in the centre of Istanbul's Taksim square.

"Welfare's reason for being is to express the protest of those left out of the system. But in power it has compromised with the central forces of the system...isolating itself from its grassroots," commentator Dogu Ergil told Reuters on Tuesday.
"Of course, optimistic economic signals helped them change this attitude," Ergil said.

Riding high amid better-than-expected budget figures, a soaring stock market and an improved outlook for privatisation, Erbakan unleashed his plans late last month on an establishment lulled to sleep by his earlier readiness to compromise.

The prime minister, secular Turkey's first Islamist leader, has also sought to exploit the vulnerability of coalition partner Tansu Ciller. Press reports have linked her True Path Party to state-sponsored death squads and the drugs trade.
The seismic shocks of Erbakan's shift prompted speculation that the armed forces, self-proclaimed guardians of the secularist order, would step into domestic politics for the fourth time in 37 years.
"Coup or Democracy?" asked columnist Ismet Berkan in the daily Radikal. Mainstream television and newspapers are full of coup speculation -- already something of a national pastime.
At the same time, Welfare's radical wing read the shift at the top as a licence to step up pressure on secular rivals across the country.

Elected Welfare officials in the Ankara district of Sincan hosted a day of anti-Israeli protests at the weekend, culminating in calls for implementation of Islamic sharia law, in violation of Turkey's secular constitution.
Pro-Welfare municipal workers later beat several journalists covering the ensuing scandal.

The staunchly secularist military responded with its own show of strength, parading 20 tanks and 15 armoured personnel carriers through the streets of Sincan on Tuesday morning. An army spokesman called it a routine training mission.

Meanwhile, Islamists in paramilitary-style uniforms have surfaced in the central city of Kayseri, another Welfare stronghold. The country's chief prosecutor has given the party 30 days to disband the formations.
And Islamist-controlled television and newspapers have taken a noticeably harder line in recent weeks.
Amid the rising tensions, Turkey's leading leftist party said on Tuesday it would file a censure motion against the Erbakan-led government to preserve the secular democracy in the country.

Bulent Ecevit, leader of the Democratic Left Party, told his parliamentary faction the motion would focus on problems of the "secular democratic republic, foreign affairs, economic and social issues and security." No date has been set for a vote.
